newsitem.title: UK: Soyoil guaranteed free of gene-soya on Euro market.
newsitem.headline: Soyoil guaranteed free of gene-soya on Euro market.

text.p: Traders on the European vegetable oil market are being offered soy oil guaranteed free from genetically modified U.S. soybeans.
"Oil is being offered which comes with three independent certificates which guarantee it is not from modified soybeans," said a trader.
The soybeans come with a certificate from the transport company which moves the beans from the farm, one from the grain elevator and one from a laboratory which has checked the beans.
One such laboratory is Iowa-based Genetic ID, founded a little over two months ago and now working at capacity with orders from brokers on both sides of the Atlantic.
A small part of this year's U.S. soybean crop, around two percent, comes from genetically-modified seed. The beans, called Roundup-ready, were developed to resist Monsanto's Roundup herbicide.
But European consumer and environmental groups have voiced concern over the use of genetically altered material and some food manufacturers in Germany say they will not use it.
Genetic ID said the genetic code of all unaltered soybean plants is identical, no matter which part of the plant is tested.

If a soybean plant has been genetically altered, which means foreign DNA has been spliced into the natural genetic sequence of the plant, it can be detected by Genetic ID's proprietary technology. This testing protocol can be applied to any crop or other organism used as a food product, the company said.
Although traders in Europe are well aware of companies like Genetic ID offering testing services they said cost was a major factor.

"The tests, plus separate transport and storage add about $15 a tonne to the cost of soybeans shipped into Europe, but the sellers can't get any more for their oil and meal than the market will allow," said a trader.
Other traders said the alteration would have come about anyway using more natural means.

"Soybeans would have become resistant to the herbicides over a period of time using cross breeding methods and no one would have known any different. All that has happen is that the process has been speeded up," said another. --Jim Ballantyne, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8062
